**La resolución (viggaha).** La resoluci: **The resolution (viggaha).** The resolution, also called viggaha-vākya, is the unfolded phrase, with the proper inflection of each member, of which the compound is the abbreviation. Moggallāna-pañcikā-ṭīkā (Sāratthavilāsinī) explains the term thus: “visesena gayhati ñāyatyaneneti viggaho … visesena vā gahaṇaṃ viggaho, tadatthaṃ vākyaṃ viggahavākyaṃ”, it is called viggaha because by means of it [the meaning] is grasped and known distinctly; or else viggaha is the distinct grasping, and the phrase that has that purpose is the viggaha-vākya (Mogg-p-ṭ., pp. 145–146). Rūpasiddhi calls the uncompounded expression vākya: “tadaññaṃ vākyam iti ruḷhaṃ”, the other [what is not a compound] is conventionally known as vākya (Rū. §331); in contrast to it, the compounded form is called vutti (sutta 364; Nir. 261). The same ṭīkā cites the difference between the two: “samāse visesanaṃ visessam anupavīsati ekībhavati visesanaṃ, vākye tu visesanaṃ visessato visuṃyevā vatiṭṭhate”, in the compound the qualifier enters into the qualified and becomes one with it; in the phrase it remains separate from the qualified (Mogg-p-ṭ., p. 145).
**byatihāralakkhaṇa**, una de las 9 clas: **byatihāralakkhaṇa**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). It indicates a reciprocal action. E.g., *daṇḍehi ca daṇḍehi ca paharitvā idaṃ yuddhaṃ pavattati ti daṇḍādaṇḍi*, a fight in which they strike one another with sticks is called *daṇḍādaṇḍi*, sticks with sticks. (Rū. §352 (p. 207))
**disantarāḷattha**, una de las 9 clases: **disantarāḷattha**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). It refers to the intermediate points of the compass. E.g., *pubbassā ca dakkhiṇassā ca disāya yad antarāḷaṃ sā ’yaṃ pubbadakkhiṇā vidisā*, that which lies between the east and the south directions, this is the intermediate direction of the south-east. (Rū. §352 (p. 207))
**dvipada-bhinnādhikaraṇa**, una de las: **dvipada-bhinnādhikaraṇa**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). It consists of two members which, before forming the compound, have different inflections. E.g., *chattaṃ pāṇimhi assa iti chattapāṇi puriso*, there is an umbrella in his hand, so he is a man with an umbrella in his hand. Here, *chatta*, umbrella, and *pāṇi*, hand, have different inflections before forming the compound. (Rū. §352 (pp. 204–205))
**nanipāta-pubbapada**, una de las 9 cla: **nanipāta-pubbapada**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). It has the particle *na* as first member. E.g., *natthi etassa puttā ti aputtako*, he has no sons, so he is (a man) without sons. (Rū. §352 (p. 205))
**saha-pubbapada**, una de las 9 clases: **saha-pubbapada**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). It has the particle *saha* as first member. This type of compound has the first inflection. E.g., *saha hetunā yo vattate ti sahetuko*, that which arises with a root is designated as having a root. (Rū. §352 (pp. 205–206))
**saṅkhyobhayapada**, una de las 9 clase: **saṅkhyobhayapada**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). In this compound the members are numerals. (Rū. §352 (pp. 206–207))
**tipada**, una de las 9 clases de compu: **tipada**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). It consists of 3 members. E.g., *sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya kāyo assa iti sīhapubbaddhakāyo*, his body is like the front half of a lion, therefore he is called one whose body is like the front half of a lion. This relative compound is formed of 3 members: (1) *sīha*, lion, (2) *pubbaddha*, front half, and (3) *kāya*, body. (Rū. §352 (p. 205))
**upamāna-pubbapada**, una de las 9 clas: **upamāna-pubbapada**, one of the 9 kinds of relative compounds (**bahubbīhi**). It has a word of comparison as first member. This compound is in the first and the sixth inflection. E.g., *kāko viya sūro ayaṃ iti kākasūro*, this one is bold like a crow, so he is called “bold as a crow”. (Rū. §352 (p. 206))

A su vez el compuesto relativo es de dos: In turn, the relative compound is of two classes: (1) Atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa, a type of relative compound where what qualifies the meaning is not brought when the meaning of the other word is brought. What qualifies the meaning is not included in the meaning of the other word. E.g., *bahudhanaṃ ānaya*, bring (the man of) much wealth. Here, what qualifies, much wealth, is not brought when the man is brought. (2) Tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa, a type of relative compound where what qualifies the meaning is brought when the meaning of the other word is brought. What qualifies the meaning is included in the meaning of the other word. E.g., *lambakaṇṇaṃ ānaya*, bring (the man who has) long ears. Here, what qualifies, long ears, is brought when the man is brought. (Rū. §352)

Compuesto copulativo colectivo. Los miem: Collective copulative compound. The members are taken as a whole and not individually; that is why, like the collective numerical compound (samāhāra-digu), this compound is in the singular and in the neuter gender. E.g., *cakkhu ca sotañ ca* = *cakkhusotaṃ*, eye and ear. (Kacc. §322; Rū. §359)
Compuesto numérico colectivo. Este tipo: Collective numerical compound. This kind of compound expresses totality and has a neuter singular ending. E.g., *tayo + lokā* = *tilokaṃ*, the three worlds (planes) collectively.
Compuesto numérico no-colectivo. Este ti: Non-collective numerical compound. This kind of compound does not express totality but the objects individually. It can have a singular or plural ending. E.g., *tayo + bhavā* = *tibhavā* (the three stages of existence).
Compuesto que denota algo diferente de l: A compound that denotes something different from what each of its members represents. *Bahubbīhi*, which means a place where there is much grain, exemplifies this type of compound (*bahu*, much, and *vīhi*, grain).[^8] The individual members are not sufficient to explain the meaning of the compound. The use of the other word (aññapada),[^9] *ya*, *ta*, *eta* and *ima*, is required for the resolution of the compound. In a relative compound the meaning of the other word predominates.
Compuestos determinativos donde la infle: Determinative compounds in which the inflection of the first member is not elided
Con el sentido de «malo» (Rū. §347): kuc: With the sense of “bad” (Rū. §347): kucchito puriso kāpuriso, kupuriso vā, contemptible man (attested: “sakkāro kāpurisena dujjaho”, Thag. 247 (PTS p. 18)); and with that of “little”: kāpupphaṃ, few flowers (Kacc. §336).
Con los derivados primarios en «tavantu»: With primary derivatives in “tavantu”, “māna”, “anta”, etc., no compound is formed: only the phrase exists. E.g., odanaṃ bhuttavā (who has eaten the rice), dhammaṃ suṇamāno, dhammaṃ suṇanto (who listens to the Dhamma) (Rū. §351 (p. 193)).
Con los nombres de árboles, hierbas, ani: With the names of trees, grasses, animals, wealth, grains and districts, etc., the copulative compound is facultatively collective: it is in the singular and in the neuter gender or, otherwise, in the plural and with the gender of the last member (*Vibhāsā rukkha-tiṇa-pasu-dhana-dhañña-janapadādīnañ ca*, Kacc. §323; Rū. §360).
Cualquier tipo de compuesto, adverbial,: Any kind of compound, adverbial, adjectival, numerical, determinative and copulative, if it is used as an adjective, becomes a relative compound. The relative compound must agree in number, gender and grammatical case with the noun it qualifies.
Cuando califica a un nombre, este compue: When it qualifies a noun, this compound has the same gender and number as what it qualifies. Examples: *so saraṇagato*, he has gone for refuge; *te saraṇagatā*, they have gone for refuge; *sā saraṇagatā*, she has gone for refuge; *tā saraṇagatāyo*, they (f.) have gone for refuge; *taṃ kulaṃ saraṇagataṃ*, that family has gone for refuge; *tāni kulāni saraṇagatāni*, those families have gone for refuge.
Cuando dos nombres se refieren a la mism: When two nouns refer to the same thing (tulyādhikaraṇa),[^6] the compound is called *kammadhāraya*,[^7] adjectival compound. Generally, in this kind of compound two different words are combined, one that qualifies (adjective) and another that is qualified (noun), which on forming the compound acquire a single meaning.
Cuando el segundo miembro comienza en vo: When the second member begins with a vowel, *ku* is substituted by *kad*. *Ku* is explained as *kucchita*, bad, contemptible. *Ku* is also substituted by *kā* to signify *appaka*, little, insufficient. But it can also have the meaning of “bad”, as in *kāpuriso*, contemptible man.
Cuando se forma un compuesto hay (1) agr: When a compound is formed there is (1) combination of words (sadda-samasana) and (2) combination of meaning (attha-samasana). In the case of a compound where the inflection of the first member is not elided (alutta-samāsa), there is only combination of meaning.[^2] But when the ending of the first member is elided (lutta-samāsa), there is both combination of words and combination of meaning.
Cuando sigue *pati*, esposo, a *jāyā*, e: When *pati*, husband, follows *jāyā*, wife, it is sometimes replaced by *tudaṃ* or by *jāni* (Kacc. §339; Rū. §358): *jāyā ca pati ca* = *tudaṃpati*, *jānipati*, wife and husband. Also *jayampatikā*, where the niggahīta is added and the vowel is shortened.[^15]
Ejemplo: *pabhaṃ karoti* = *pabhaṅkaro*,: Example: *pabhaṃ karoti* = *pabhaṅkaro*, making light, the sun (Kacc. §317; Rū. §332).

El canon lo escribe con di-, dentro del: The canon writes it with di-, within the copulative compound “dirattatirattaṃ”: “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anupasampannena dirattatirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappetuṃ” (V. ii 27 (PTS Vin iv 16)). El compuesto (samāsa) se considera como: The compound (samāsa) is regarded as part of the noun (nāma) because it is generally a combination of nouns that are mutually related and because it depends on the noun.[^1]
El compuesto adjetivo (kammadhāraya) y e: The adjectival compound (kammadhāraya) and the numerical compound (digu) are also called determinative compound (tappurisa-samāsa) (Kacc. §326; Rū. §341), in which the meaning of the last member is predominant; moreover, the gender is determined by the last member and, unlike the adverbial compound, they can be singular and plural and take different inflections.
El compuesto copulativo es colectivo, po: The copulative compound is collective, by rule and not facultatively, when its members signify parts of beings, musical instruments, parts of a vehicle, parts of an army, small creatures, different enemies and things different but alike (visabhāga),[^17] etc. (*Tathā dvande pāṇitūriyayoggasenaṅga-khuddajantuka-vividhaviruddha-visabhāgatthādīnañ ca*, Kacc. §322; Rū. §359). However, forms such as *hatthapādā*, hands and feet, and *maṃsalohitāni*, flesh and blood, are explained as an individual copulative compound (Rū. §359).[^18]
El compuesto es de seis clases (saññāvas: The compound is of six classes (saññāvasena chabbidho; Rū., p. 176):
El compuesto exige que los significados: A compound requires the meanings to be connected (yuttattha). In “bhaṭo rañño, putto devadattassa” (the soldier of the king, the son of Devadatta) “rājaputto” is not formed, because “rañño” is related to “bhaṭo” and not to “putto”. In “kosalassa rañño putto” (the son of the king of Kosala) it is not formed either, because “rañño” needs another word (sāpekkha). But with relational nouns (sambandhī-sadda) there is a compound, because the sense is understood: devadattassa gurukulaṃ (the house of Devadatta’s teacher), bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho (the community of disciples of the Bhagavā) (Kacc. §316; Rū. §351 (p. 197)).
El miembro que califica, *thera*, *ācari: The qualifying member, *thera*, *ācariya*, teacher, *paṇḍita*, sage, etc., is placed at the end.
El primer miembro es la partícula 'na',: The first member is the particle ‘na’, not. This negative particle is replaced by ‘a’ before a consonant and by ‘an’ before a vowel. E.g., *na* + *kusala* = *akusala*, not wholesome, unwholesome; *na* + *ariyo* = *anariyo*, not noble, ignoble.
El primer miembro está en la quinta infl: The first member is in the fifth inflection. It is used to indicate the meanings: separation or moving outwards (apagamana), fear or danger (bhaya), abstinence (virati), release (mocana), etc. (Rū. §351 (pp. 195–196))
El primer miembro está en la segunda inf: The first member is in the second inflection. E.g., *gāmaṃ* + *gato* = *gāmagato*, who has gone to the village. The second member is *gata*, gone, *nissita*, depending, *atīta*, past, *atikkanta*, surpassing, *patta*, reaching, *āpanna*, entering, etc. (Rū. §351 (pp. 191–193))
El primer miembro está en la sexta infle: The first member is in the sixth inflection. It is used to indicate possession. (Rū. §351 (pp. 196–197))
El primer miembro está en la séptima inf: The first member is in the seventh inflection. (Rū. §351 (pp. 197–198))
El primer miembro está en la tercera inf: The first member is in the third inflection. The second member is a primary derivative (kitaka), *pubba* (previous), *sadisa* (similar), *sama* (equal), *ūna* (deficient, less), *kalaha* (dispute), *nipuṇa* (skilled, adept), *missa* (mixed), *sakhila* (affable). (Rū. §351 (pp. 193–194))
El primer miembro tiene la cuarta inflex: The first member has the fourth inflection. It is used to indicate purpose (tadattha), for (attha), benefit, welfare (hita), what is to be given (deyya), etc. (Rū. §351 (pp. 194–195))
El segundo miembro es una comparación y: The second member is a comparison, and the particle *viya*, like, is used to explain the second member. E.g., *sīho viya sīho*, lion (means) like a lion.
El siguiente es un paradigma de las posi: The following is a paradigm of the possible inflections of the compound *upanagaraṃ* (Kacc. §341; Rū. §336).[^4] This paradigm applies to other adverbial compounds ending in *aṃ*, such as *upakumbhaṃ*, near the water pot, etc.
En *a-brāhmaṇa*, como un brahmán. Éste e: In *a-brāhmaṇa*, like a brahmin. This is another use of the particle of negation when it forms a compound. This is called *pariyudāsa*, rejecting the meaning of the last member of the compound after taking up what is similar; that is, it indicates similarity. In the preceding example, *a-brāhmaṇa*, like a brahmin (similar to, but not, a brahmin); *an-assa*, like a horse (= donkey, mule); *amanussa*, like a human (= spirit, deity); *assamaṇo*, like a monk (similar to, but not, a monk).
En *a-sūriya-passā rājadārā*, las esposa: In *a-sūriya-passā rājadārā*, the king’s wives do not see the sun, the particle *a* negates *passā*, see, and not *sūriya*, sun. This is one of the uses of the particle of negation when it forms a compound with other words. This is called *pasajjappaṭisedha*, preventing after reaching. That is, the particle *a* ignores *sūriya*, sun, and negates the last member of the compound, *passā*, see. Other examples: *akatvā*, not having done; *puññaṃ akaronto*, not doing merit.
En *apunageyyā gāthā*, verso que no ha d: In *apunageyyā gāthā*, a verse that is not to be recited again, and *alavaṇabhojī*, (a person) who does not eat salt, the particle of negation is not connected in meaning with the following member but with the last member of the compound. These kinds of compounds are called *ayuttattha-samāsa*, a kind of compound whose members are not connected in meaning.
En *mātāpitaro* y *pitāputtā* la *u* fin: In *mātāpitaro* and *pitāputtā* the final *u* of the first member (*mātu*, *pitu*) becomes *ā* in the copulative compound, by the rule *Tesu vuddhi…* (Kacc. §404; Rū. §370).
En compuesto, ante «liṅga», etc., «puma»: In a compound, before “liṅga”, etc., “puma” loses its final a (Kacc. §222; Rū. §342), and the m becomes niggahīta (Kacc. §82; Rū. §149: “Aṃ-mo niggahitaṃ jha-la-pehi”). This is how Nandisena derives it at Kacc. §222: “Puṅkokilo = puma + kokilo (‘a’ of ‘puma’ is elided (§222); ‘m’ is substituted by ‘ṃ’ (§82); ‘ṃ’ is substituted by ‘ṅ’ (§31))”; the last step is “Vaggantaṃ vā vagge” (Kacc. §31). Rūpasiddhi gives “punnāgo” in the same way (Rū. §342).
En el canon aparecen en plural, como com: In the canon they appear in the plural, as individual copulative compounds: *dve jāyampatikā*, two spouses (S. i 322 (PTS ii 98)), where the VRI edition reads *jāyampatikā* and notes the variant *jayampatikā*; and *Te honti jānipatayo* (A. i 370 (PTS ii 59)). *Tudaṃpati* is not found in the canonical texts of the Sixth Council edition; only in the grammars and in a ṭīkā that refers to Kaccāyana.
En el canon el compuesto copulativo apar: In the canon the copulative compound appears in the Therīgāthā: *Sītuṇhena ca ḍayhantī*, tormented by cold and heat (Thī. 393 (PTS p. 135)), which the Aṭṭhakathā resolves as *sītena ca uṇhena ca* (ThīA. 125 (PTS p. 121)). The resolution without a compound is also in the canon: *Yo ’dha sītañ ca uṇhañ ca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati* (D. iii 151 (PTS iii 185)).
En el canon: *Aguttaṃ cakkhusotasmiṃ*, d: In the canon: *Aguttaṃ cakkhusotasmiṃ*, unguarded in the eye and the ear (A. i 284 (PTS i 281)), with the seventh inflection singular of the paradigm. Rūpasiddhi notes that sometimes the collective compound is not neuter, as the form *aṃmo* of the aphorism *Aṃ-mo niggahitaṃ jha-la-pehi* (Kacc. §82; Rū. §149) shows; thus *ādhipaccaparivāro*, *chandapārisuddhi*, *paṭisandhippavattiyaṃ* (Rū. §359). Suttaniddesa also gives *cittuppādo* (Suttaniddesa, ad Kacc. §82).
En el canon: *Pesalā Sāriputtamoggallānā: In the canon: *Pesalā Sāriputtamoggallānā*, Sāriputta and Moggallāna are of good conduct (S. i 151 (PTS i 149)), and the locative *Sāriputtamoggallānesu* in the same passage; *Yathā vā pan’ eke bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā* (D. i 6 (PTS i 6)); *tāva naṃ dakkhanti devamanussā*, for so long will devas and human beings see him (D. i 42 (PTS i 46)); *yato ca candimasūriyā uggacchanti* (D. i 226 (PTS i 240)); *mātāpitaro sukhenti pīṇenti* (D. i 48 (PTS i 51)). When the compound depends on *yuga*, pair, the canon uses it in the singular: *Sāriputtamoggallānaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ*, the pair of disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna (D. ii 4 (PTS ii 5)); Saddanīti points this out (Sad. (Smith p. 768)).
En el canon: *samathavipassanaṃ yuganadd: In the canon: *samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāveti*, he develops tranquillity and insight yoked together (A. i 475 (PTS ii 157)), as against the resolution *samatho ca vipassanā ca* (D. iii 179 (PTS iii 213)); *viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ* (D. ii 28 (PTS ii 32)); *tibbaṃ me hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati* (S. i 420 (PTS ii 220)).
En el canon: «Sabbe aniccā tibhavā upadd: In the canon: “Sabbe aniccā tibhavā upaddutā” (Thag. 360 (PTS p. 102)). Saddanīti points out that the digu is neuter and singular only “as a rule” (yebhuyyena), and quotes, from the usage of the poets, “tibhavo khāyate tadā”, in the masculine singular.
En el compuesto copulativo [generalmente: In the copulative compound [generally] the more honoured [member] and the one with fewer vowels come first; sometimes, the one ending in *i* or in *u*; [and] the one ending in *a* that begins with a vowel; when they are many, there is no fixed rule.
En el compuesto, «rājan» puede tomar ‘a’: In the compound, “rājan” may take a final ‘a’ by “Kvaci samāsantagatānam akāranto” (Kacc. §337; Rū. §350), and it is then declined like “purisa”: devarājo, devarājaṃ, devarāje. If it does not take it, it is declined like “rājā”: so devarājā, te devarājāno. The same happens with devānaṃ sakhā: devasakho or devasakhā (Rū., p. 196).
En este tipo cada miembro conserva su pr: In this type each member keeps its own meaning and predominates (avayavappadhāna); that is why the compound is always in the plural [except when it depends on “yuga”, pair: see the note], in all the inflections, and has the gender of the last member: *Sāriputtamoggallānā*, *Sāriputtamoggallāne*, *Sāriputtamoggallānehi*, etc. (Rū. §357)[^14]
En este tipo de compuesto cualquiera de: In this type of compound either of the two members can come first, because the qualifier and the qualified are ordered at will: chando jāto assā ti chandajāto, or jātachando; likewise chinnahattho or hatthacchinno (Rū. §352 (p. 202)).
En este tipo de compuesto el primer miem: In this kind of compound the first member is a noun, in any inflection except the first (nominative or vocative), explaining or determining the second member. There are six kinds: (1) in the second inflection (dutiyā-tappurisa), (2) in the third inflection (tatiyā-tappurisa), (3) in the fourth inflection (catutthī-tappurisa), (4) in the fifth inflection (pañcamī-tappurisa), (5) in the sixth inflection (chaṭṭhī-tappurisa) and (6) in the seventh inflection (sattamī-tappurisa). (Kacc. §327; Rū. §351)
In this kind of compound the first member, the indeclinable, predominates. The second (last) member of the compound generally has the neuter first inflection (aṃ) and is indeclinable.
En estos nombres, «guṇa» no significa «v: In these names, “guṇa” does not mean “virtue” but the qualifier: it is the secondary meaning of the members of the compound, which, because it qualifies the meaning of the other word, is called “its quality” (tagguṇa); and “saṃviññāṇa” is being understood together with: tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa is the relative compound in which the meaning of the other word is understood together with its qualifier, without leaving it (“tagguṇaṃ amuñcitvā tagguṇena sah’ eva viññāṇo aññapadattho yasmin ti tagguṇasaṃviññāṇo”, Nir. 129; cf. Rū. §352 (p. 200)). U Sīlānanda also explains it thus (Rūpasiddhi class no. 47).
En guḷodano y assaratho la resolución ll: In guḷodano and assaratho the resolution contains a word that does not appear in the compound (saṃsaṭṭho, yutto); Niruttidīpanī calls this “majjhepadalopo”, elision of the middle word, and resolves in the same way “maggena sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ maggacittaṃ” (sutta 345; Nir. 225). Moggallāna explains why the compound is valid even though that word is missing: “vuttipadenevopasittādikiriyāyākhyāpanato natthāyuttatthatā”, since the compound form itself expresses the action (upasitta, etc.), there is no lack of connection of meaning (Mogg., p. 120).
En la edición del Sexto Concilio, CST, e: In the Sixth Council edition, CST, the beginning of the Samāsakaṇḍa is on p. 176.
En la primera inflexión. D. ii 15 (PTS i: In the first inflection. D. ii 15 (PTS ii 18).
En la quinta inflexión no hay terminació: In the fifth inflection there is no ending in *aṃ*; in the third, sixth and seventh the inflection *aṃ* is optional; in the remaining inflections the ending is only *aṃ*.
En la resolución de este tipo de compues: In the resolution of this kind of compound another term is used, which explains the meaning of the prefix.
En la resolución, el pronombre «ta» toma: In the resolution, the pronoun “ta” takes the gender of the first member: “mahanto ca so puriso ca”, “nīlañ ca taṃ uppalañ ca”, “brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā ca” (Kacc. §324), also when the second member is of another gender: “mukhañ ca taṃ cando ca” (Rū., p. 187), “vinayo ca so pariyatti ca”, “avijjā ca sā paccayo ca”, “sīlañ ca taṃ guṇo ca” (Niruttidīpanī p. 126). This is how U Sīlānanda teaches it (Kaccāyana class no. 8).
En la sexta inflexión, con elisión del ú: In the sixth inflection, with elision of the last member (uttarapadalopa). “Kumāro suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco”, D. ii 15 (PTS ii 17).
En las dos resoluciones de Rūpasiddhi (R: In Rūpasiddhi’s two resolutions (Rū. §348 (p. 190); Kacc. §325), it is the word “samāhaṭā” or “samāhāro” that distinguishes the collective from the non-collective in the resolution: without it, Rūpasiddhi resolves in the same way “catasso disā catuddisaṃ”, collective, and “catasso disā catuddisā”, non-collective (Rū., p. 191), and only the number and gender of the compound show the kind.
En los compuestos de números el número m: In compounds of numbers the smaller number comes first: *ekakadukaṃ*, *dukatikaṃ*, *tikacatukkaṃ*. In *dāsidāsaṃ* the middle vowel is shortened (*dāsī* → *dāsi*).
En los ejemplos anteriores la otra palab: In the preceding examples the other word is the subject (kattā); in chinnarukkho it is the instrument (karaṇa): “Evaṃ kattari. Karaṇe pana chinno rukkho yenā ti chinnarukkho, pharasu” (Nir. 246). Payogasiddhi also places it separately, “karaṇatthe”.
En los ejemplos anteriores, *diṭṭha*, *s: In the preceding examples, *diṭṭha*, *suta* and *gata* have an active meaning. In the following examples, the meaning is passive.
En los tres ejemplos anteriores, *Saṃghā: In the three preceding examples, *Saṃghārāmo*, monastery of the Saṃgha, *Sāvatthī* and *Jetavana* are what is denoted (abhidheyya) by the compound and the other word (aññapada), in this case *imaṃ*. Because they are in the meaning of the second inflection, this type of compound is said to belong to the second inflection.
En los tres, la vocal final se acorta po: In all three, the final vowel is shortened because the compound is neuter (Kacc. §342; Rū. §337): itthī → adhitthi, vadhū → upavadhu; in “upagu”, the “o” of “go” is shortened to “u” (“okārassa rassattaṃ ukāro”, Rū. §338).
En pubbarattaṃ, la ‘i’ final de «ratti»: In pubbarattaṃ, the final ‘i’ of “ratti” becomes ‘a’ by “Kvaci samāsantagatānam akāranto” (Kacc. §337). Of the same type: accantaṃ (antaṃ atikkantaṃ, which goes beyond the limit), paccakkhaṃ (akkhaṃ patigataṃ, present before the eyes), pubbanhaṃ (ahassa pubbaṃ, the earlier part of the day, the morning), where “aha” is replaced by “anha”; Niruttidīpanī and the canon write pubbaṇha. Rūpasiddhi also admits the normal order: haṃsarājā alongside rājahaṃso, māsaddhaṃ alongside addhamāsaṃ (Rū. §351 (p. 198)).
En rigor, es el compuesto entero el que: Strictly speaking, it is the whole compound that is regarded as neuter (“So napuṃsakaliṅgo”, Kacc. §320; Rū. §335), and after an adverbial compound ending in “a” the inflections become “aṃ” only “sometimes” (kvaci; Kacc. §341; Rū. §336): hence the optional forms in -ena, -ehi, -ā, -assa, etc., in the following paradigm. After one not ending in “a” the inflections are elided (Kacc. §343; Rū. §338).
En «khattiyakaññā», «rattalatā» y «brāhm: In “khattiyakaññā”, “rattalatā” and “brāhmaṇadārikā”, the first member is a feminine that indicated masculine (bhāsitapuma) and, before a feminine last member that refers to the same thing, it is regarded as masculine and loses the feminine suffix: khattiyā → khattiya, brāhmaṇī → brāhmaṇa (Kacc. §332; Rū. §343). This holds only for the first member: in “khattiyakumārī” or “taruṇabrāhmaṇī” the last member keeps the feminine suffix. And it does not apply if the word is not used in the masculine: “gaṅgānadī”, “pathavīdhātu” (Rū. §343).
En «mahābalaṃ», «mahanta» se sustituye p: In “mahābalaṃ”, “mahanta” is replaced by “mahā” before a word that refers to the same thing (Kacc. §330; Rū. §340). In “mahabbhayaṃ” it is replaced by “maha”: the sutta says “mahataṃ”, in the plural, and thereby teaches that the substitution is sometimes “maha” (Rū. §340); Rūpasiddhi gives no step beyond this (Rū., p. 184: “mahabbhayaṃ, mahaādeso”). Tipiṭaka: “Satto saṃsāram āpādi, dukkham assa mahabbhayaṃ” (S. i 34 (PTS i 37)).
En «pacanacaṇḍāla», «pacana» no es aquí: In “pacanacaṇḍāla”, “pacana” does not mean “cooking” here. According to U Sīlānanda (Rūpasiddhi class no. 50), it is said figuratively of those who harm other beings, as if they burned them, such as those who kill sheep, pigs, birds and game animals (orabbhika, sūkarika, sākuṇika, māgavika); and “caṇḍāla” is the name of a group of people who did despised work, such as tending the cemeteries and burning the corpses. Rūpasiddhi and Niruttidīpanī give the class and its examples without explaining the name (Rū. §359 (p. 212); Niruttidīpanī p. 135).
En «pādapo», como en «urago» (urena gacc: In “pādapo”, as in “urago” (urena gacchatī ti, that which goes with the chest, the snake), there is only the compound (vutti); the resolution is made with the verb. Conversely, sometimes there is only the phrase and no compound is formed: parasunā chinnavā (who has cut with the axe), kākehi pātabbā (which crows can drink), dassanena pahātabbā (which are to be abandoned by seeing) (Rū. §351 (p. 194)).
En «subhikkhaṃ» la «ā» final de «bhikkhā: In “subhikkhaṃ” the final “ā” of “bhikkhā” is shortened because the compound is neuter (Kacc. §342; Rū. §337), and the inflection becomes “aṃ” (Kacc. §341; Rū. §336). Rūpasiddhi treats this example precisely under “Saro rasso napuṃsake”. In the canon: “subhikkhaṃ bhavissati, dubbhikkhaṃ bhavissati”, there will be abundance of food, there will be scarcity (D. i 10 (PTS i 11)).
Es decir, no deja nada aparte («na kiñci: That is, he leaves nothing aside (“na kiñci parivajjetī ti attho”, Rū. §338). In the canon: “Sakaṇṭakaṃ so gilati, jaccandho ’va samakkhikaṃ”, [the king who punishes without examining] swallows [the food] with thorns, as one blind from birth [eats] with flies (J. i 253, Mahāpaduma-jātaka; JA. iv 192 (PTS iv 192)).
Es el paradigma que da Rūpasiddhi (§349): This is the paradigm Rūpasiddhi gives (§349): “Tilokaṃ, he tiloka, tilokaṃ, tilokena, tilokassa, tilokā tilokasmā tilokamhā, tilokassa, tiloke tilokamhi tilokasmiṃ”. There is only the singular, because in the collective “sabbatth’ ekavacanam eva hoti” (Rū. §349); Niruttidīpanī sums it up thus: “Imasmiṃ samāhāradigumhi sabbaṃ napuṃsakam eva rassantam eva ekavacanantam eva”. The examples that follow, all ending in -a, are declined in the same way.
Este compuesto es facultativo (vibhāsā),: This compound is facultative (vibhāsā), so that it is sometimes not formed: “puṇṇo Mantāniputto”, “citto gahapati”, “sakko devarājā” (Rū. §339; Nir. 234 adds “brahmā sahampati”).
Este compuesto no debe confundirse con e: This compound must not be confused with the adjectival compound in which both members are qualifiers (visesanobhayapada), see above. In the adjectival compound the two members refer to the same thing (tulyādhikaraṇa) and the resolution has the pronoun *ta*: *sītañ ca taṃ uṇhañ ca* = *sītuṇhaṃ*, (something that is) cold and hot. In the copulative compound each member refers to a different thing and the resolution has only *ca*: *sītañ ca uṇhañ ca* = *sītuṇhaṃ*, cold and heat.[^12]
Este ejemplo no está en Rūpasiddhi; Niru: This example is not in Rūpasiddhi; Niruttidīpanī gives it among the visesanuttarapada, with “purisavaro” and “purisaviseso” (Nir. 234). Tipiṭaka: “Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama” (D. iii 160 (PTS iii 197)).
Este tipo consiste en dos miembros que s: This type consists of two members that refer to the same thing and are in the same inflection. There are 6 classes according to the inflection of the other word (aññapada): (i) in the second inflection, (ii) in the third inflection, (iii) in the fourth inflection, (iv) in the fifth inflection, (v) in the sixth inflection, (vi) in the seventh inflection.[^11]
Este tipo de compuesto se denomina *alop: This type of compound is called *alopa-tappurisa* or *alutta-tappurisa*, determinative compound without elision.
Este tipo de compuesto se denomina *amād: This type of compound is called *amādipara-tappurisa*, a determinative compound that has as its last member a word ending in *aṃ*, etc. That is, there is a transposition between the members of the compound. (Rū. §351 (p. 198))
Este tipo de compuesto tiene un indeclin: This kind of compound has an indeclinable (abyaya)—a prefix (upasagga) or a particle (nipāta)—as its first member.[^3]
Este tipo de compuesto tiene un numeral: This kind of compound has a numeral as its first member and can be included within the category of adjectival compounds because both members are in the same inflection.
Este tipo de compuesto une dos o más nom: This type of compound joins two or more nouns that are in the same inflection, that refer to different things and that are connected in meaning (yuttattha). In the resolution each member is followed by the particle *ca*, and; in the compound the particle is not used, because the compound itself already expresses that meaning (*vuttatthānam appayogo*, what has already been expressed is not used). E.g., *Sāriputto ca Moggallāno ca* = *Sāriputtamoggallānā*, Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Formación (Rū. §350): dve rattiyo → dvi: Formation (Rū. §350): dve rattiyo → dvi + ratti (kammadhāraya, Kacc. §324; Rū. §339; elision of the inflections, Kacc. §317; Rū. §332; original form, Kacc. §318; Rū. §333) → digu (Kacc. §325; Rū. §348), singular and neuter (Kacc. §321; Rū. §349) → dviratta (Kacc. §337; Rū. §350) → dviratta + si → dviratta + aṃ (“Si ’ṃ”, Kacc. §219; Rū. §195) → dvirattaṃ (the preceding a is elided, “Saralopo…”, Kacc. §83; Rū. §67). Kacc. §337 says “kvaci” (sometimes), and Rūpasiddhi reads it in two ways, both of which give dviratta: (1) the final vowel becomes “a”, which is what Kaccāyana’s vutti says: dviratti → dviratta; (2) “a” is a suffix (a ca ko ca akā), and then the preceding vowel is elided by “Saralopo…” (Kacc. §83; Rū. §67): dviratti + a → dviratt + a = dviratta. This second reading is the one Rūpasiddhi details for dvirattaṃ. The same holds for tisso rattiyo tirattaṃ, dve aṅguliyo dvaṅgulaṃ and satta godāvariyo sattagodāvaraṃ: according to Rūpasiddhi, Kacc. §337 applies here to the end of ratti, aṅguli and godāvarī. Payogasiddhi gives rules of its own for these words after a numeral.
Hay compuestos que son siempre compuesto: There are compounds that are always compounds (niccasamāsa) and others that are not (aniccasamāsa) (Sad. (Smith p. 745)); the one that is always a compound is not resolved with its own words: “niccayamāsāna maviggaho [read niccasamāsānam aviggaho], asakapadaviggaho vā yutto”, it befits the obligatory compound to have no resolution, or to have one with a word not its own (Mogg-p-ṭ., p. 147). Thus the adverbial compound: nagarassa samīpaṃ, upanagaraṃ, near the city, with samīpaṃ in place of upa (see note 3). The vutti of Kaccāyana, by contrast, resolves it as nagarassa samīpe pavattati kathā iti upanagaraṃ, the talk that arises near the city [is called] upanagaraṃ (Kacc. §319); the words added in this way are known “samāsasāmatthiyena”, by the force of the compound (sutta 336; Nir. 217).
Hay dos clases: (1) colectivo (samāhāra-: There are two kinds: (1) collective (samāhāra-digu) and (2) non-collective (asamāhāra-digu).
Hay nueve clases (Rū., p. 183; Sad. (Smi: There are nine kinds (Rū., p. 183; Sad. (Smith p. 751)):
Hay nueve clases de compuesto relativo:: There are nine classes of relative compound: (1) two members which have the same location (dvipada-tulyādhikaraṇa), (2) two members which do not have the same location (dvipada-bhinnādhikaraṇa), (3) three members (tipada), (4) the particle *na* is the first member (nanipāta-pubbapada), (5) *saha* is the first member (saha-pubbapada), (6) the first member is a comparison (upamāna-pubbapada), (7) both members are numerals (saṅkhyobhayapada), (8) it refers to the intermediate points of the compass (disantarāḷattha), (9) it indicates a reciprocal action (byatihāralakkhaṇa).[^10]
Hetupaccayo es la primera de las veintic: Hetupaccayo is the first of the twenty-four conditions, Paṭṭh. i 1 (“Hetupaccayo, ārammaṇapaccayo, adhipatipaccayo…”).
Jinavacanaṃ (la Palabra del Conquistador: Jinavacanaṃ (the Word of the Conqueror): Jinassa (of the Conqueror) vacanaṃ (word)
Kacc. §321 (Rū. §349) «Diguss’ ekattaṃ»:: Kacc. §321 (Rū. §349) “Diguss’ ekattaṃ”: “Digussa samāsassa ekattaṃ hoti, napuṃsakaliṅgattañ ca”—the digu is in the singular and in the neuter gender. Rūpasiddhi resolves the compound in two ways: “tayo lokā samāhaṭā cittena sampiṇḍitā” (the three worlds gathered together, grouped by the mind) or “tiṇṇaṃ lokānaṃ samāhāro” (the gathering of the three worlds). And it specifies that the rule applies to the collective: “Samāhāradiguss’ etaṃ gahaṇaṃ”.
Kacc. §325 (Rū. §348) «Saṅkhyāpubbo digu: Kacc. §325 (Rū. §348) “Saṅkhyāpubbo digu”: “Saṅkhyāpubbo kammadhārayasamāso digusañño hoti”—the adjectival compound (kammadhāraya, Kacc. §324; Rū. §339) that has a numeral as its first member receives the name “digu”. By Kacc. §326 (Rū. §341) “Ubhe tappurisā”, the digu and the kammadhāraya also receive the name “tappurisa”.
Kacc. §335, en la edición publicada, res: Kacc. §335, in the published edition, resolves kudārā as a relative compound (bahubbīhi): “kucchitā dārā yesaṃ te hontī ti kudārā”, those who have bad wives. Saddanīti—Sad. (Smith p. 753)—admits both resolutions (“kucchitā dārā kudārā … atha vā kucchitā dārā yesaṃ te kudārā”); here the adjectival compound resolution is followed.
Kacc. §337 lo da entre los ejemplos de l: Kacc. §337 gives it among the examples of the final “a” (“pañca ahāni pañcāhaṃ, sattāhaṃ”). In the canon: “bhagavā bodhirukkhamūle sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisīdi” (V. iii 1 (PTS Vin i 1)); “bhagavā sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinno hoti” (Ud. 77 (PTS p. 1)).
Kaccāyana ilustra compuestos relativos q: Kaccāyana illustrates relative compounds that contain other compounds, e.g. sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā isayo: “This is a relative compound which has the same location (tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi) and which has a copulative compound and an adjectival compound in it (dvanda-kammadhāraya-gabbho)” (Kacc. §328).
La característica es la de Rūpasiddhi: «: The characteristic is that of Rūpasiddhi: “bhinnatthānaṃ ekatthībhāvo samāsalakkhaṇaṃ”, that words of different meanings come to have a single meaning (Rū. §331). Saddanīti attributes it to “some” (keci) and gives another as its own: “nānāpadānaṃ ekapadattūpagamanaṃ samāsalakkhaṇaṃ”, that several words come to be a single word (Sad. (Smith p. 745)).
La colección (samuccaya), es decir, la a: The collection (samuccaya), that is, the act of bringing together (sampiṇḍana), is of four kinds according to meaning: (1) simple collection (kevalasamuccaya), (2) secondary addition (anvācaya), (3) union of one with another (itarītarayoga) and (4) collective (samāhāra). In the first two no compound is formed, because each noun depends on the verb and not on the other nouns: *cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātañ ca paccayaṃ sayanāsanaṃ adāsi*, he gave the robe, the food, the requisite [of medicines] and the lodging (simple collection); *dānañ ca dehi, sīlañ ca rakkhāhi*, give gifts and guard morality (secondary addition). The compound is formed only in the last two, because in them the nouns are connected with one another.[^13]
La diferencia entre este tipo de compues: The difference between this kind of compound and the copulative compound (**dvanda**) is that in the latter each member is taken individually. E.g., *sītañ ca uṇhañ ca* = *sītuṇhaṃ*, cold and heat.
La frase sin componer, con la tercera in: The uncompounded phrase, with the third inflection, is found in the definition of the First Noble Truth: “piyehi vippayogo pi dukkho” (D. ii 243 (PTS ii 305)).
La inflexión no se elide por el «ca» de: The inflection is not elided owing to the “ca” of “Tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ca” (Kacc. §317; Rū. §332), as Rūpasiddhi explains (Rū., p. 199). E.g., pabhaṅkaro (pabhaṃ karotī ti, maker of light), attanopadaṃ (voice for oneself).
La lista de diez significados no está en: The list of ten meanings is not in Rūpasiddhi, which distinguishes only the senses of similar, other, opposite and absence (“taṃsadisatadaññatabbiruddhatadabhāvesu pi”, Rū. §344 (p. 188)). It coincides, in the same order, with a stanza quoted by the Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā (ApA. ii 143 (PTS p. 430): “paṭisedhe vuddhitabbhāve…pe… akāro virahappake’’ ti evaṃ vuttesu dasasu atthesu”) and given in full by Sīmavisodhanī (p. 49): “Paṭisedhe vuddhitabbhāve, aññatthe sadise pi ca; viruddhe garahe suññe, akāro viraha’ppake”. Several of the examples (amanusso, anudarā kaññā, asekkhā dhammā) are in the analysis of negation in the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā (Vis-ṭ. ii 264), with other terminology.
La palabra «sampayuttaṃ» de la resolució: The word “sampayuttaṃ” in the resolution is from Niruttidīpanī.
La partícula de negación *a* puede tener: The negative particle *a* can have the following meanings:
La regla es *Nāmānaṃ samuccayo dvando*:: The rule is *Nāmānaṃ samuccayo dvando*: the collection (samuccaya) of nouns [having the same inflection] has the name *dvanda* (copulative compound) (Kacc. §329; Rū. §357). In this compound the meaning of both members predominates (ubhayapadatthappadhāna). Rūpasiddhi explains the name: *dve dve padāni dvandā*, words in twos are called *dvanda*, pair; owing to its resemblance to a pair, this compound is also called *dvanda*.
La resolución «dhammo iti buddhi» muestr: The resolution “dhammo iti buddhi” shows that “dhammabuddhi” is not “the understanding of the dhamma” —that would be “dhammassa buddhi”, a determinative compound in the sixth inflection— but the understanding of something as dhamma; so also “dhammasaññā”, the perception [of something] as dhamma (Rū., p. 187). “Dhamma” and “buddhi” are different things; as U Sīlānanda explains (Rūpasiddhi class no. 43), the particle “iti” brings the first member to the level of the second, so that the two refer to the same thing.
La vocal del medio se alarga por Kacc. §: The middle vowel is lengthened by Kacc. §403 (Rū. §354) and the final one becomes i by “Tesu vuddhi…” (Kacc. §404). Neither kesākesi nor daṇḍādaṇḍi is found in the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries of the Sixth Council; only in the grammars.
La vocal final de dvi pasa a ā por «Dv’-: The final vowel of dvi becomes ā by “Dv’-ek’-aṭṭhānam ākāro vā” (Kacc. §383) and is then shortened (Rū.); the doubling of t (dvatti-) is not mentioned by Rūpasiddhi. Cf. “dvattipattapūrā paṭiggahetabbā”, V. ii 108 (PTS Vin iv 80).
Las gramáticas asignan tagguṇa o atagguṇ: The grammars assign tagguṇa or atagguṇa to each example, not to each class according to the inflection. Niruttidīpanī gives chinnahattho puriso as tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa and dinnasuṅko rājā as atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa (Nir. 242). Saddanīti calls āgatasamaṇo saṃghārāmo atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa, and jitindriyo samaṇo tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa, because the ascetic is taken together with his faculties, which are part of him (Sad. (Smith p. 760)).
Las nueve clases de kammadhāraya las enu: The nine kinds of kammadhāraya are listed by Rūpasiddhi when introducing Rū. §339 (= Kacc. §324, “Dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe kammadhārayo”), p. 183; the sambhāvanāpubbapada, on p. 187. Saddanīti gives them at §702: Sad. (Smith pp. 751–752).
Los dos miembros califican a una tercera: The two members qualify a third thing, which may remain expressed: “siniddho ca so uṇho cā ti siniddhuṇho” māso, (bean) oily and hot (Rū., p. 186); “gilāno ca so vuṭṭhito cā ti gilānavuṭṭhito”, “gilāno hutvā gelaññā vuṭṭhito”, one who was ill and has recovered (Sad. (Smith p. 751)). Other examples from Rūpasiddhi: khañjakhujjo, chiddāvachiddaṃ, uccāvacaṃ, chinnabhinnaṃ.
Los dos, con «tiropākāraṃ», están atesti: The two, together with “tiropākāraṃ”, are attested together in the description of the supernormal power: “tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati seyyathā pi ākāse”, he passes unhindered to the other side of a wall, of a rampart, of a mountain, as though through space (D. i 73 (PTS i 78)).
Los siguientes compuestos se denominan *: The following compounds are called *upapada-samāsa* or *upapada-tappurisa*. This special kind of compound does not admit a resolution like the other compounds.
Los tres últimos (maggaṭṭho, kucchisayo,: The last three (maggaṭṭho, kucchisayo, paṅkajaṃ) are upapada: there is only the compound, as in vanacaro (vane caratī ti, who wanders in the forest) and thalaṭṭho (which stands on dry land). Conversely, in “bhojane mattaññutā” (moderation in eating), “indriyesu guttadvāratā” (guarding of the doors of the senses) and “āsane nisinno” (seated on the seat) there is only the phrase, without a compound (Rū. §351 (pp. 197–198)).
Moggallāna da para las dos primeras otro: For the first two Moggallāna gives other examples: *dhave ca khadire ca palāse ca chinda*, cut the dhava, the khadira and the palāsa (simple collection), and *bhikkhañ cara gāvo cānaye*, go for alms and bring the cows (secondary addition). Niruttidīpanī (sutta 357; Nir. 251) does not wholly accept the restriction: simple collection also forms a compound, as in *cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ* (M. i 39 (PTS i 33)), and so does secondary addition, as in *mālāgandhavilepanadhāraṇamaṇḍanavibhūsanaṭṭhānā* (D. i 5 (PTS i 5)).
Moggallāna no admite «tudaṃpati». Da «ja: Moggallāna does not admit “tudaṃpati”. He gives “jayampatī”, and “jānipatī”, “dampatī”, “jampatī” as distinct words, not as substitutions of “jāyā”: “‘jānipatī’ ti pakatantarena siddhaṃ, tathā ‘dampatī, jampatī’ ti” (Moggallāna, p. 137). According to its ṭīkā, the Pañcikā expressly excludes the usage “tudampati”, and with “aññehi ca”, “and by others”, refers to Rūpasiddhi: “nā ’yam payogo ti tudampatippayogaṃ nivattetvā … aññehi cā ti iminā rūpasiddhiṃ gaṇhāti” (Moggallāna-pañcikā-ṭīkā, M p. 185).
Na pasa a a por «Attaṃ nassa tappurise»: Na becomes a by “Attaṃ nassa tappurise” (Kacc. §333), taken separately (yogavibhāga).
Niruttidīpanī entiende *dīghamajjhimaṃ*: Niruttidīpanī understands *dīghamajjhimaṃ* differently: it places it in a class of its own, that of the collections of one and the same recitation (ekasaṅgītidvanda), together with *aṅguttarasaṃyuttakaṃ* and *khandhakavibhaṅgaṃ*; that is, the Dīgha and the Majjhima. In the canon, collective compounds of this class and of the next appear together in a single passage: *Puttabhariyaṃ … dāsidāsaṃ jātidhammaṃ, ajeḷakaṃ jātidhammaṃ, kukkuṭasūkaraṃ jātidhammaṃ, hatthigavāssavaḷavaṃ jātidhammaṃ, jātarūparajataṃ jātidhammaṃ* (M. i 217 (PTS i 162)); and *pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahesuṃ* (M. i 228 (PTS i 171)).
No se forma compuesto con los derivados: No compound is formed with the derivatives in “tabba” and “tuṃ”: saṅghassa dātabbaṃ (which is to be given to the Order), saṅghassa dātuṃ (to give to the Order) (Rū. §351 (p. 195)).
No tiene sutta propio. Según Rūpasiddhi,: It has no sutta of its own. According to Rūpasiddhi, “Pādipubbapado ca niccasamāso ’va” (Rū., p. 189): it is always a compound, and the resolution is made with another word that gives the sense of the prefix (padhānaṃ, bhusaṃ, vividhā, adhiko, sobhanaṃ…). Niruttidīpanī (Nir. 239) points out the lengthening in pāvacanaṃ (“pakaṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ pāvacanaṃ, dīghattaṃ”).
No todos los compuestos adverbiales se r: Not all adverbial compounds are resolved with another word (see note 3). Several compounds in this table are resolved with the same particle: “pāsādassa anto”, “mañcassa heṭṭhā” (Rū., p. 182), “bhattassa pacchā”, and also, in the first table, “addhamāsaṃ addhamāsaṃ anu” (Rū., p. 181). Others, such as upanagaraṃ (“nagarassa samīpaṃ”) and yathāvuḍḍhaṃ (“vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭipāṭi”), are resolved only with another word. This is how U Sīlānanda explains it (Rūpasiddhi class no. 42).
No traspasando el significado de la pala: Not going beyond the meaning of the word (padatthānatikkama)
Orden de los miembros. Generalmente el m: Order of the members. Generally the more honoured member (accitatara) is placed first: *Sāriputtamoggallānā*, *samaṇabrāhmaṇā*, *devamanussā*, *mātāpitaro*. Sometimes the member with fewer vowels (appasara) is placed first: *cando ca sūriyo ca* = *candasūriyā*, the moon and the sun; *nigamā ca janapadā ca* = *nigamajanapadā*, towns and districts. Sometimes the member ending in *i* or in *u* is placed first: *aggi ca dhūmo ca* = *aggidhūmā*, fire and smoke; *dhātavo ca liṅgāni ca* = *dhātuliṅgāni*, roots and bases. Sometimes, between members ending in *a*, the one beginning with a vowel is placed first: *attho ca dhammo ca* = *atthadhammā*, the meaning and the Dhamma; also *atthasaddā* or *saddatthā*, the meaning and the word. When the members are many, there is no fixed order. (Rū. §357–§358)
Otro sentido, fuera de la lista: mera pa: Another sense, outside the list: mere particle (nipātamatta): khipiṃ anantakaṃ (Vv. 108 (PTS p. 117); VvA. 290 (PTS p. 309)), I put into his hand the rag [in which I carried the gruel tied up] (anantakaṃ = nantakaṃ, “rag”); na cā pi apunappunaṃ (J. i 34), nor ever again.
Otros ejemplos (Rū., p. 201). Rūpasiddhi: Other examples (Rū., p. 201). Rūpasiddhi gives them without resolution; that of khīṇāsavo follows the model of chinnahattho, and that of dasabalo is that of Kacc. §328.
Otros ejemplos (Rū., p. 207): pubbuttarā: Other examples (Rū., p. 207): pubbuttarā (north-east), aparadakkhiṇā (south-west), pacchimuttarā (north-west). Here there is no treatment of the feminine as masculine (pumbhāvātidesa), because no word having the same locus follows; the final vowel of the first member is shortened by Kacc. §403 (Rū. §354). If “dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā ca” is understood, it is an adjectival compound (kammadhāraya), and then that treatment does occur, and so does the pronominal declension: dakkhiṇapubbassā, dakkhiṇapubbassaṃ (Rū., p. 207).
Otros ejemplos (Rū., pp. 205–206). En sa: Other examples (Rū., pp. 205–206). In sahetuko, saha becomes sa by “Tesu vuddhi…” (Kacc. §404) and ‘ka’ is added by “Kvaci samāsantagatānam akāranto” (Kacc. §337); sahetu is also correct. “Hetu c’ eva sahetuko ca”, Dhs. 218 (PTS p. 192).
Para la resolución de este tipo de compu: For the resolution of this kind of compound the particle *iti*, thus, is used. This particle “raises” the first member to the level of the second. *hutvā*, *bhūta*, being, are also used.

For the resolution of this kind of compound, and to show that both members refer to the same thing, the pronoun-article *ta*, this one (masc./fem.), and the particle *ca*, and, are used. The compound *mahāpuriso*, great man, is resolved as follows:
Para resolver este tipo de compuesto se: To resolve this kind of compound the particle *eva*, itself, is used. The first member restricts the second member.
Paradigma de declinación aplicable a tod: Declension paradigm applicable to all collective compounds.
Por eso dice Rūpasiddhi: «So ca niccasam: That is why Rūpasiddhi says: “So ca niccasamāso ti assapadaviggaho”, and this, being an obligatory compound (niccasamāsa), is resolved with words that are not its own (assapadaviggaha; Saddanīti writes “asapada-”) (Rū., p. 176; Sad. (Smith p. 752)). According to Suttaniddesa, the adverbial compound is obligatory “in most cases” (yebhūyyena), and there are a few that are not, such as “majjhe samuddasmiṃ” and “tiro pabbataṃ” (Suttaniddesa, ad Kacc. §319).
Por la palabra *ādi*, etc., Rūpasiddhi i: By the word *ādi*, etc., Rūpasiddhi here also includes opposites (aññoññappaṭipakkhadhamma) and birds (sakuṇa):[^20]
Por la palabra *ādi*, etc., del aforismo: By the word *ādi*, etc., of the aphorism, Rūpasiddhi also includes: nouns distinguished by gender (aññoññaliṅgavisesita), numbers and measures (saṅkhyāparimāṇa), people of low standing (pacanacaṇḍāla) and directions (disā). (Rū. §359)
Por lo tanto, hay dos clases de compuest: Therefore there are two kinds of copulative compound: (1) individual (itarītarayoga-dvanda) and (2) collective (samāhāra-dvanda). (Rū. §357)
Resolución de Rūpasiddhi (§350); Nirutti: Rūpasiddhi’s resolution (§350); Niruttidīpanī also gives “eko puggalo ekapuggalo”. In the canon: “Ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjati bahujanahitāya” (A. i 21 (PTS i 21–22)).
Resolution of complex compounds. A compound that contains other compounds (gabbha) is resolved in steps, each with its own resolution, and the last step gives the class of the whole. Rūpasiddhi resolves in this way nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu, [the mountain] of valleys perfumed by the flowers fallen from various trees: “nānappakārā dumā nānādumā, nānādumehi patitāni nānādumapatitāni, nānādumapatitāni ca tāni pupphāni cā ti nānādumapatitapupphāni, tehi vāsitā nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā, nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā sānū yassa pabbatassa so ’yaṃ nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu pabbato. Ayaṃ pana kammadhārayatappurisagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi”, this is a relative compound which has the same location and which contains an adjectival compound and a determinative compound (Rū., pp. 203–204). The vutti of Kaccāyana gives a dozen similar cases, almost all with a second resolution as a relative compound which does not have the same location (bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi): “Vāsitā sānū vāsitasānu; sāpekkhatte sati pi gamakattā samāso”, perfumed valleys [are called] vāsitasānu; although it is looking to another place, because it can convey the meaning, it is a compound (Kacc. §328).
Rūpasiddhi (p. 190) da a continuación es: Rūpasiddhi (p. 190) then gives these compounds, and also pahāro, parābhavo, vihāro, āhāro, upahāro. Saddanīti—Sad. (Smith p. 753)—, which takes them from its teachers (garū), observes that in diṭṭhapubbo and the others the two members are not seen to refer to the same thing (tulyādhikaraṇa), and that the reason why they are adjectival compounds remains to be sought.
Rūpasiddhi (§344, p. 188) lo resume en u: Rūpasiddhi (§344, p. 188) sums it up in a stanza: “Pasajjappaṭisedhassa, lakkhaṇaṃ vatthunatthitā; vatthuto aññatra vutti, pariyudāsalakkhaṇaṃ”, the characteristic of pasajjappaṭisedha is the non-existence of the thing; the characteristic of pariyudāsa is the application to something other than the thing. Niruttidīpanī (Nir. 237) specifies that pasajjappaṭisedha negates only the action (kriyāmattanisedha: akatvā, akātuṃ, akaronto) and pariyudāsa negates the thing (dabbanisedha: abrāhmaṇo, asamaṇo, amitto).
Rūpasiddhi (§349) da además: tayo daṇḍā: Rūpasiddhi (§349) also gives: tayo daṇḍā tidaṇḍaṃ (three sticks), tilakkhaṇaṃ (three characteristics), catasso disā catuddisaṃ (four directions), pañcasikkhāpadaṃ (five training rules), saḷāyatanaṃ (six āyatana), navalokuttaraṃ (nine supramundane [dhammas]), dasasīlaṃ (ten precepts), and, with the “a” of Kacc. §337, tirattaṃ, dvaṅgulaṃ, sattagodāvaraṃ and pañcagavaṃ. In catuddisaṃ, the ā of disā is shortened by Kacc. §342 (Rū. §337) “Saro rasso napuṃsake”: Kaccāyana states it for the abyayībhāva, but Rūpasiddhi warns that “abyayībhāva” is not to be carried over into it, so that the shortening also holds in the neuter digu, dvanda and bahubbīhi. Catuddisaṃ is found in the canon: “cattāro naṃ devaputtā catuddisaṃ rakkhāya upagacchanti” (D. ii 11 (PTS ii 12)).
Rūpasiddhi añade que también en el compu: Rūpasiddhi adds that the two combinations may also occur in the compound without elision, because its members come to be a single word: “tatth’ āpi vā ekapadattūpagamanato duvidham pi labbhat’ eva” (Rū. §331); Nyāsa ad Kacc. §316 says the same. Saddanīti gives as examples of combination of meaning in compounds without elision “dūre-nidānaṃ”, “gavam-pati”, “urasi-lomo” and “devānaṃ-piya-Tisso” (Sad. (Smith p. 741)).
Rūpasiddhi añade: «Bhinnappavattinimittā: Rūpasiddhi adds: “Bhinnappavattinimittānaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ visesanavisesitabbabhāvena ekasmiṃ atthe pavatti tulyādhikaraṇatā”, that is, there is tulyādhikaraṇatā when two words that apply for different reasons (pavattinimitta) apply to a single thing, one as the qualifier (visesana) and the other as the qualified (visesitabba) (Rū. §339; likewise in Sad. (Smith p. 751)).
Rūpasiddhi cierra el capítulo de compues: Rūpasiddhi closes the chapter on compounds with two stanzas that classify it in another way. By the member whose meaning predominates, the compound is of four classes: in which the meaning of the first member predominates (pubbapadatthappadhāna), of the last member (uttarapadatthappadhāna), of both (ubhayapadatthappadhāna) or of another word (aññapadatthappadhāna); with the numerical compound and the adjectival compound, of six. They are, respectively, the adverbial compound, the determinative compound, the copulative compound and the relative compound (Sad. (Smith pp. 746, 754, 759, 768); for the adverbial and the determinative, also Rū. §330 (p. 178) and §341 (p. 184)). By its subdivisions, the adverbial compound is of two classes, the adjectival compound of nine, the numerical compound of two, the determinative compound of eight, the relative compound of nine and the copulative compound of two: in all, thirty-two (caturaṭṭhadhā, “four times eight”) (Rū., pp. 214–215). The Kaccāyana tradition counts twenty-seven (the adjectival compound of six classes and the relative of seven) and, according to some, twenty-eight if the determinative compound of the first inflection is added (Suttaniddesa, ad Kacc. §316; cf. Sad. (Smith p. 745), “sattavīsatividho aṭṭhavīsatividho”).
Rūpasiddhi cuenta *kusalākusalaṃ* entre: Rūpasiddhi counts *kusalākusalaṃ* among the facultative ones (Rū. §360), and Kaccāyana likewise places *sāvajjānavajjaṃ*, *hīnapaṇītaṃ* and *kaṇhasukkaṃ* under the *ādi* of this aphorism (Kacc. §323). By contrast, for Saddanīti it is a case of the different enemies (vividhaviruddha) (Sad. (Smith p. 750)), and Niruttidīpanī (sutta 358; Nir. 253) places it among the opposites (vividhaviruddha), which it distinguishes from the enemies (niccaveri); for both, the collective is obligatory. In the canon the plural appears only as a qualifier (*kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipākā*, Dhs. 145 (PTS p. 124)); as a noun it appears in the singular: *saṃkhittena kusalākusalaṃ desetu*, may he teach me kusala and akusala briefly (M. ii 157 (PTS i 489)). Other attestations: *rājā pasenadi kosalo kāsikosalaṃ ajjhāvasati* (D. i 217 (PTS i 227)); *pahūtaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ ohāya* (D. i 108 (PTS i 115)); *imaṃ rattindivaṃ vītināmeyya* (M. i 16 (PTS i 13)); *Ahorattaṃ anuyuñjaṃ* (S. i 123 (PTS i 122)).
Rūpasiddhi cuenta ocho clases de *tappur: Rūpasiddhi counts eight kinds of *tappurisa* (“Digu dudhā tappuriso, aṭṭhadhā …”, Rū., p. 215): these six, plus the *amādipara-tappurisa* and the *alopa-tappurisa*, which are treated further below as “irregular determinative compounds” and “determinative compounds in which the inflection of the first member is not elided”.
Rūpasiddhi da además: vividho kappo, vis: Rūpasiddhi also gives: vividho kappo, visiṭṭho vā kappo vikappo, diverse or special arrangement (= alternative); adhidevo, adhisīlaṃ; sundaro gandho sugandho, good smell; asobhanaṃ kataṃ dukkaṭaṃ, badly done. Sukataṃ and dukkaṭaṃ, together in Dh. 58 (PTS p. 45): “Akataṃ dukkaṭaṃ seyyo, pacchā tappati dukkaṭaṃ; katañ ca sukataṃ seyyo, yaṃ katvā n’ ānutappati”.
Rūpasiddhi da catasso disā en las dos cl: Rūpasiddhi gives catasso disā in both kinds: catuddisaṃ (collective, neuter, with the final vowel shortened) and catuddisā (non-collective, feminine plural). It adds as non-collective ekadhammo (one dhamma), ekaputto (one son) and dasasahassacakkavāḷāni (ten thousand world systems). Catuddisā in the canon: “balavā saṅkhadhamo appakasiren’ eva catuddisā viññāpeyya” (D. i 234 (PTS i 251)).
Rūpasiddhi da dos razones para tratar el: Rūpasiddhi gives two reasons for treating the compound immediately after the noun: because it depends on the noun (nāmanissitattā) and because it is itself nominal (sayañ ca nāmikattā) (Rū., p. 176). In Kaccāyana, the chapter on compounds is a section of the chapter on the noun: “Iti nāma-kappe samāsa-kappo sattamo kaṇḍo”.
Rūpasiddhi da este ejemplo como visesana: Rūpasiddhi gives this example as visesanapubbapada and writes it “hetuppaccayo” (Rū., p. 186); the Paṭṭhāna writes “hetupaccayo”. Niruttidīpanī, on the other hand, places it among the sambhāvanāpubbapada: “Hetu hutvā paccayo hetupaccayo”, the condition that is a root (Nir. 234).
Rūpasiddhi da la razón: en el upapada-sa: Rūpasiddhi gives the reason: in the upapada-samāsa “there is only the compound (vutti), because it is obligatory (nicca)” (Rū. §351 (p. 193)). Therefore the resolution is made with the verb (“kammaṃ karotī ti kammakāro”) and not with the two members of the compound. Niruttidīpanī says this of the primary derivatives formed with an object as preceding member: “niccasamāso yeva” (Nir. 224).
Rūpasiddhi da también «antevāsī», junto: Rūpasiddhi also gives “antevāsī”, alongside “antevāsiko”; both are in the canon, e.g. “suppiyassa pana paribbājakassa antevāsī brahmadatto māṇavo” (D. i 1 (PTS i 1)).
Rūpasiddhi da también «pubbenivāsānussat: Rūpasiddhi also gives “pubbenivāsānussati”, which is the first of the three vijjā: “pubbenivāsānussati ñāṇaṃ vijjā” (Dhs. 265 (PTS p. 234)).
Rūpasiddhi da también «puṇḍarīkam iva pu: Rūpasiddhi also gives “puṇḍarīkam iva puṇḍarīko, samaṇo ca so puṇḍarīko cā ti samaṇapuṇḍarīko” (Rū., p. 187). Tipiṭaka: “Katamo ca puggalo samaṇapadumo? Idh’ ekacco puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmī hoti…”, followed by “samaṇapuṇḍarīko” (Pu. 173 (PTS p. 63)).
Rūpasiddhi da también «tiṇṇaṃ malānaṃ sa: Rūpasiddhi also gives “tiṇṇaṃ malānaṃ samāhāro” (§349). The only occurrence of timalaṃ in the canon, “Ekamūlaṃ dvirāvaṭṭaṃ, timalaṃ pañcapattharaṃ” (S. i 30 (PTS i 32)), is not this numerical compound but a bahubbīhi qualifying taṇhā: “Sā ca rāgādīhi tīhi malehi timalā” (SA. i 79 (PTS i 84)).
Rūpasiddhi dice que este tappurisa toma: Rūpasiddhi says that this tappurisa takes the number and gender of what it denotes (abhidheyyavacanaliṅga), because “gata”, etc., are primary derivatives and have the three genders (Rū. §351 (p. 193)). When the last member is a noun of fixed gender, the compound keeps the gender of that noun: rājaputto, rukkhamūlaṃ, itthirūpaṃ. Niruttidīpanī says this of the whole type: “abhidheyyavacano parapadaliṅgo ca”, the number of what is denoted and the gender of the following member (Nir. 231).
Rūpasiddhi explica por qué «saṃghārāmo»: Rūpasiddhi explains why “saṃghārāmo” does not take the second inflection: āgata and samaṇa give up their own meaning and are applied to that of the other word, which is that of the second inflection; “saṃghārāmo” is added only to clarify that meaning, and since the compound already expresses the meaning of the object, the second [inflection] is not repeated. The pronoun “imaṃ” is not used with the compound, and so in all cases (Rū. §352 (p. 200)); in the example, Rūpasiddhi (p. 200) and Niruttidīpanī (VRI ed.) read “āgatasamaṇā sāvatthi”, as the Sixth Council edition generally writes the nominative (e.g. M. i 200 (PTS i 146): “yena sāvatthi tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi”); here “Sāvatthī” is written, the form of the feminine stem in -ī, as in Sad. (Smith p. 760).
Rūpasiddhi lo explica así: «Así como el: Rūpasiddhi explains it thus: “Just as the object (kamma) holds two things, the action and its purpose—because if there is an object there is an action and there is a purpose—so this compound holds two names of a single thing, because if there is a compound there are two names that express a single meaning” (Rū. §339; likewise in Sad. (Smith p. 751)). Suttaniddesa illustrates it with “kaṭaṃ karoti”, he makes a mat: the object, the mat, holds the action of making it and its purpose, sitting on it (Suttaniddesa, ad Kacc. §324).

Rūpasiddhi no da estos dos ejemplos. Nir: Rūpasiddhi does not give these two examples. Niruttidīpanī admits them and gives the collective alongside: “dve satāni dvisataṃ … tisahassaṃ”, or else “dvisatāni, dve satāni … tisahassāni, tīṇi sahassāni”, “evaṃ vacanadvayañ ca vākyañ ca veditabbaṃ”; and it answers the objection that here both members are numerals: in the digu the first member must be a numeral, the second may or may not be one.
Rūpasiddhi plantea la dificultad en una: Rūpasiddhi raises the difficulty in a stanza: “Na nisedho sato yutto, desādiniyamaṃ vinā; asato c’ āphalo tasmā, katham abrāhmaṇo ti ce?”, it is not appropriate to negate what exists without specifying the place, etc., and to negate what does not exist is useless; then how [can one say] “abrāhmaṇo”? And it answers: “Nisedhatthānuvādena, paṭisedhavidhi kvaci; parassa micchāñāṇattā-khyāpanāyopapajjate”, sometimes negation, repeating what is negated, is appropriate for making known to another that his knowledge is mistaken (Rū. §344 (p. 187)). As U Sīlānanda explains (Rūpasiddhi class no. 43), one says “he is not a brahmin” to someone who takes for a brahmin a person who only looks like one; that is why Rūpasiddhi concludes: “abrāhmaṇo ti brāhmaṇasadiso ti vuttaṃ hoti”, “abrāhmaṇo” means “resembling a brahmin” (Rū., p. 188).
Saddanīti da esta misma resolución («cat: Saddanīti gives this same resolution (“cattāri saccāni samāhaṭāni catusaccaṃ”, Sad. (Smith p. 754)), with a single s, as do Niruttidīpanī and Payogasiddhi; Rūpasiddhi writes catussaccaṃ. In the canon catusaccaṃ predominates: “Catusaccaṃ pakāsento, varadhammappavattako” (Ap. i 121 (PTS i 109)); with double s it is found only once: “Tajjito brahmadaṇḍena, catussaccaṃ apāpuṇi” (V. iv 490 (PTS Vin ii 293)).
Saddanīti distingue las dos clases por l: Saddanīti distinguishes the two classes by the resolution: it is tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa “yattha avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho”, when it is resolved with the part and the sense of the compound is the whole (lambakaṇṇo); and atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa “yattha pana samudāyena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho”, when it is resolved with the whole (bahudhano) (Sad. (Smith p. 760)).
Saddanīti explica con este compuesto que: Saddanīti uses this compound to explain that the adverbial compound may be indeclinable only in part (ekadesena): “samuddassa majjhe majjhe-samuddaṃ, tasmiṃ majjhe-samuddasmiṃ”, with the seventh inflection, as in the verse “Ko ’yaṃ majjhe samuddasmiṃ, apassaṃ tīram āyuhe” (Sad. (Smith p. 746); J. ii 159 (Mahājanaka-jātaka); JA. vi 44 (PTS vi 35)). The Sixth Council edition prints “majjhe samuddasmiṃ” as two words.
Saddanīti llama a estos compuestos de do: Saddanīti calls these compounds of double interpretation (dvādhippāyika): “sītañ ca taṃ uṇhañ cā ti sītuṇhaṃ” bhattaṃ, cold and hot food, is kammadhāraya; “sītañ ca uṇhañ ca sītuṇhaṃ”, cold and heat, as in “sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanati”, is dvanda; and “katākataṃ” and the like are also resolved in both ways (Sad. (Smith p. 753)).

Se declina en singular según el paradigm: It is declined in the singular following the paradigm of *tilokaṃ*, which applies to all collective compounds (see the numerical compound): *cakkhusotaṃ, he cakkhusota, cakkhusotaṃ, cakkhusotena*, etc. (Rū. §359).[^16]
Se dice que hay dos ventajas en la forma: Two advantages are said to exist in the formation of a compound: (1) the condition of being a single word and (2) the condition of having a single inflection (ekapadatta, ekavibhattitta; Rū. §331).
Según Rūpasiddhi (p. 190), estos nombres: According to Rūpasiddhi (p. 190), these nouns, particles and prefixes for which no rule has been given are compounded by division of the sutta “nāmānaṃ samāso” (Kacc. §316, Rū. §331), because, not being connected in meaning, they cannot be compounded by any other rule (“ayuttatthattā n’ āññena samāso”). Niruttidīpanī (Nir. 238) attributes it to the wide scope of the rule (“bahulādhikārā ayuttatthānam pi samāso hoti”) and also gives the resolution that turns them into compounds of connected meaning: “puna gāyitabbā ti punageyyā, na punageyyā apunageyyā”.
Según Rūpasiddhi, el calificativo va al: According to Rūpasiddhi, the qualifier goes at the end so as not to contradict the word of the Jina (jinavacanānuparodhato), that is, because the text says so. The reverse order also occurs: “ācariyaguttilo” (Rū., p. 186; Sad. (Smith p. 751)).
Según Rūpasiddhi, se llaman así por su s: According to Rūpasiddhi, they are so called because of their resemblance to the word “tappurisa” itself (“tassa puriso”, his man), in which the meaning of the last member predominates; and this compound takes the number of what it denotes (abhidheyyavacana) and the gender of the last member (paraliṅga) (Rū. §341).
Según Rūpasiddhi, «ca» y «ta» se emplean: According to Rūpasiddhi, “ca” and “ta” are used in the resolution to make clear that the two words refer to the same thing; once the compound is formed they are no longer used, because the compound itself expresses this: what has already been expressed is not used (vuttatthānam appayogo) (Rū. §339).
Sobre el nombre «digu» Rūpasiddhi da dos: On the name “digu” Rūpasiddhi gives two explanations. (1) “Dve gāvo digu”: “digu” is the compound “two cows”, and this compound is so called because of its resemblance to that word (digusadisattā). Saddanīti specifies the resemblance: the word “digu” has a numeral in front and is neuter and singular, and the same holds, as a rule (yebhuyyena), for this compound. (2) It is known (gato, avagato) by two features (dvīhi lakkhaṇehi): having a numeral as its first member and being neuter and singular; or else “it proceeds by two features” (dvīhi lakkhaṇehi gacchati pavattati). Niruttidīpanī adds that in “digu” the o of “go” becomes u.
Sobre «Dhanumh’ ā ca» (Kacc. §340; Rū. §: On “Dhanumh’ ā ca” (Kacc. §340; Rū. §355). At the end of a compound there is the suffix ‘ā’ after dhanu, and the u becomes v by “Vam od-udantānaṃ” (Kacc. §18): gāṇḍīvo dhanu yassa so ’yaṃ gāṇḍīvadhanvā (one who has a bow with many joints). By the “ca”, also after dhamma: paccakkhadhammā. According to Rūpasiddhi it occurs only sometimes (kvaci): sahassathāmadhanu, paccakkhadhammo (Rū., p. 203), and it reads gāṇṭhivadhanvā.
Sobre «Itthiyaṃ bhāsitapum’-itthī pumā ’: On “Itthiyaṃ bhāsitapum’-itthī pumā ’va ce” (Kacc. §331; Rū. §353) and “Kvac’ ādi-majjh’-uttarānaṃ dīgha-rassā paccayesu ca” (Kacc. §403; Rū. §354). In dīghajaṅgho, from dīghā jaṅghā yassa, the first member is a feminine that indicated masculine (bhāsitapuma) and it is followed by a word in the feminine having the same locus; it is treated as masculine, so that it loses the feminine suffix: dīgha (§331). And, since it is a relative compound in the masculine, the final vowel of the last member is shortened: jaṅgha (§403). Thus dīghajaṅgho puriso, a man with long legs; likewise pahūtajivho Bhagavā and mahāpañño, the latter with mahā by “Mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade” (Kacc. §330) (Rū., pp. 202–203). This does not occur if the feminine word is not used in the masculine: saddhādhuro (Rū., p. 203).
Sobre «Nadimhā ca» (Kacc. §338; Rū. §356: On “Nadimhā ca” (Kacc. §338; Rū. §356). At the end of a compound there is the suffix ‘ka’ after a word called nadī—according to Rūpasiddhi, a term of other grammarians for feminines in ī and ū—and, by the “ca”, also after what ends in tu; according to Rūpasiddhi, it is obligatory (niccatthaṃ vacanaṃ). Before ‘ka’ the vowel of the nadī is shortened by Kacc. §403 (Rū. §354): bahū nadiyo asmiṃ, bahunadiko janapado (a district that has many rivers); likewise bahujambukaṃ vanaṃ and, with tu, bahukattuko deso (Rū., p. 204). Rūpasiddhi does not mention here the change of bahū to bahu.
Son Kacc. §333 (Rū. §344), «Attaṃ nassa: These are Kacc. §333 (Rū. §344), “Attaṃ nassa tappurise”, and Kacc. §334 (Rū. §345), “Sare an”. Rūpasiddhi first forms the adjectival compound (na brāhmaṇo) and gives it the name of determinative compound by “Ubhe tappurisā” (Kacc. §326, Rū. §341), because the two suttas operate only in a tappurisa.
Son Kacc. §335 (Rū. §346), «Kad kussa»,: These are Kacc. §335 (Rū. §346), “Kad kussa”, and Kacc. §336 (Rū. §347), “Kā ’ppatthesu ca”; the sense of “bad” with “kā” is given by the plural of the sutta (“bahuvacanuccāraṇato kucchitatthe ca kvaci”). According to Rūpasiddhi this compound is always a compound (nicca-samāsa), and therefore it is resolved with another word: “kucchitam annan ti niccasamāsattā aññapadena viggaho” (Rū., p. 189). Before a consonant “ku” is retained: kudārā, kuputtā, kudāsā, kudiṭṭhi are the counter-examples to “sare” in Rū. §346.
Suttaniddesa explica el nombre: el compu: Suttaniddesa explains the name: the compound is called sambhāvana because its resolution (“guṇo iti buddhi”) is joined to the particle “iti”, which shows the consideration (“it is guṇa”). Niruttidīpanī (Nir. 235) defines sambhāvanā as “the exaltation of the meaning of the last member, which is general, by making it firm; it shows its specific nature, not a mere quality”. Its examples are those with “hutvā” and “bhūta” (hetu hutvā paccayo hetupaccayo; ariyabhūto saṅgho ariyasaṅgho), from which the last two of this section come; and of the examples with “iti” brought forward by the teachers (garū; the edition refers to Rū. §343) —dhammabuddhi, dhammasaññā, aniccasaññā, attadiṭṭhi…— it says that they fit better as determinative compounds in the first inflection with “iti” elided, like saraṇaṅgato. Rūpasiddhi, for its part, does not put hetuppaccayo in this class, but among the examples of visesanapubbapada that follow Rū. §343 (p. 186: puratthimakāyo, purāṇavihāro…).
Sólo compuesto (vutti yeva) y sólo frase: Only the compound (vutti yeva) and only the phrase (vākyam eva). With upapada, a primary derivative as second member, the phrase is not used: “upapadasamāse pana vutti yeva tassa niccattā” (kammaṃ karotī ti kammakāro, atthaṃ kāmetī ti atthakāmo) (Rū. §351 (p. 193); Kacc. §327); likewise urago, pādapo, kammajaṃ, vanacaro (Rū., pp. 194, 196, 197). With the participles in -tavantu, -māna and -anta the compound is not used: “tavantumānantādikitantehi vākyam eva … odanaṃ bhuttavā, dhammaṃ suṇamāno” (Rū., p. 193); also “parasunā chinnavā, kākehi pātabbā, dassanena pahātabbā” (Rū., p. 194). Saddanīti gives a reason: “asukhuccāraṇe aviditatthe ca vākyam eva”—only the phrase when the compound would be difficult to pronounce or its sense would not be understood—(Sad. (Smith p. 742)).
También se denomina *nicca-samāsa*, siem: It is also called *nicca-samāsa*, always a compound; this means that the members of the compound cannot be separated and still have the same meaning. E.g., *upa-nagaraṃ*, near the city; this meaning is obtained only when the two components (*upa* and *nagara*) form a compound; it is not possible to obtain this meaning by separating the two members as *upa nagaraṃ* or *nagaraṃ upa*. To express that meaning (near the city) a word different from the one used in the compound must be used; *upanagaraṃ* is defined as *nagarassa samīpaṃ*. In this case *samīpaṃ*, near, is the other word.
Tienen el mismo género, número y caso qu: They have the same gender, number and case as what is denoted (abhidheyya).

Tres maneras de resolver el compuesto ad: Three ways of resolving the adjectival compound, according to Niruttidīpanī: “mahā ca so puriso cā ti mahāpuriso”; with mahanta and without auxiliary words, “mahanto puriso mahāpuriso”; or in full, “mahanto ca so puriso cā ti mahāpuriso” (sutta 346; Nir. 233). It also explains what each auxiliary word indicates: “dvīhi casaddehi dvinnaṃ padānaṃ sakatthanānāttaṃ dīpeti. Taṃsaddena sakatthanānātte pi sakatthānaṃ adhikaraṇabhūtassa dabbatthassa ekattaṃ dīpeti” (sutta 346; Nir. 233): the two “ca” show that each word has its own meaning; “ta”, that both meanings reside in a single thing. That is why they disappear in the compound, which already expresses that unity (Rū. §339, p. 184).
Un compuesto es una abreviación de palab: A compound is an abbreviation of words (samāso padasaṅkhepo; Kacc. §316; Rū. §331). Generally each of the components of the compound, except the last member, loses its inflection. In *rāja-putto*, son of the king, the inflection of the first member *rāja*, king, is elided. Therefore, in order to understand a compound correctly, its “resolution” (viggaha, vākya) into its constituent parts is required; *rāja-putto*, son of the king, is “resolved” into *rañño*, of the king, and *putto*, son. Moreover, the resolution of the compound makes it possible to know the class to which the compound belongs, because each class of compound has a peculiar form of resolution.
Un mismo compuesto puede admitir más de: One and the same compound may admit more than one resolution and, with them, more than one class; Saddanīti calls them “dvādhippāyika” (Sad. (Smith p. 753)) and warns: “yo yo yujjati, so so attho nayaññūhi gahetabbo”, whichever sense fits, that is the one those who know the method should take (Sad. (Smith p. 748)). Which reading a passage has is decided not by grammar, which only shows that both are possible, but by the text and its commentary. The resolution also exists for primary (kitaka) and secondary (taddhita) derivatives.

«Pubbapadatthappadhāno hi abyayībhāvo»:: “Pubbapadatthappadhāno hi abyayībhāvo”: in the adverbial compound the meaning of the first member predominates (Rū. §330). Rūpasiddhi explains the name in two ways: “abyayānaṃ atthaṃ vibhāvayatī ti abyayībhāvo”, because it makes manifest the meaning of the indeclinables, or “anabyayaṃ abyayaṃ bhavatī ti”, because what is not indeclinable becomes indeclinable (Rū. §330). According to Suttaniddesa, the predominance of the first member holds “in most cases” (yebhuyyavasena), and there are adverbial compounds in which the last member or another word predominates (Suttaniddesa, ad Kacc. §319).
